title: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital

learn.hook: Reliance, Infosys and Tata Steel outlive their founders and are owned by lakhs of shareholders who never meet. What makes such a creature possible?
points: A company is an artificial person created by law, with a separate legal entity distinct from its members – it can own property, sue and be sued in its own name.
Perpetual succession: members may come and go, but the company continues.
Limited liability: in a company limited by shares, a member's liability is limited to the unpaid amount on his shares.
Common seal: traditionally the company's official signature (now optional under the Companies Act, 2013). Shares of a public company are freely transferable.
Separation of ownership and management: shareholders own the company, but an elected Board of Directors manages it.

example.q: Priya holds 100 shares of ₹10 each in a company, on which ₹7 per share has been paid. The company goes into heavy debt. What is the most she can be asked to pay?
steps: Limited liability: only the unpaid amount on her shares can be claimed.
example.answer: ₹300 – her personal assets are otherwise safe.

learn.reallife: Lakhs of Indians hold shares of companies through demat accounts; they own a slice of the company, while professional boards and managers run it.

teach.praise: Wonderful! Separate entity, perpetual succession, limited liability and management by directors.

learn.hook: Private, public, one-person, government, holding, subsidiary, associate – company labels can feel like a cricket team's batting order. Let's set the line-up.
points: By liability: company limited by shares (liability up to unpaid amount on shares), company limited by guarantee (liability up to the amount members undertake to contribute on winding up), unlimited company (no limit).

By membership: private company – minimum 2 and maximum 200 members (excluding employee/ex-employee members), restricts transfer of shares and cannot invite the public to subscribe; public company – minimum 7 members, no maximum; One Person Company – only one person as member.
Government company: at least 51% of paid-up share capital is held by the Central Government and/or State Government(s).
Holding and subsidiary: a holding company controls the composition of the subsidiary's Board of Directors or controls more than half of its total voting power.

Associate company: a company over which another has significant influence – control of at least 20% of total voting power or of business decisions under an agreement – but which is not its subsidiary.

example.q: The Government of India holds 60% of the paid-up share capital of a company. Classify it.
steps: The test for a government company is at least 51% of paid-up share capital held by government(s).

learn.reallife: Companies like Coal India and ONGC are government companies, while a solo founder's start-up may begin life as a One Person Company.

learn.hook: Two shareholders, same company: one gets a fixed 8% dividend first, the other gets whatever is left – and the vote. Which would you choose?
points: A share is a unit of a company's share capital. Shares are movable property, transferable as provided in the articles.
Preference shares carry two preferential rights: dividend at a fixed rate before equity holders, and repayment of capital before equity holders on winding up.

Types: cumulative (unpaid dividend accumulates) vs non-cumulative; participating (share surplus profits) vs non-participating; convertible vs non-convertible into equity; redeemable vs irredeemable. Under the Companies Act, 2013, a company cannot issue irredeemable preference shares.
Equity shares are those that are not preference shares. They carry residual rights to profit and capital, normal voting rights, and a dividend that varies with profits.

example.q: A company has 10,000 8% cumulative preference shares of ₹100 each. It paid no dividend last year. This year it decides to pay preference dividend. How much is due?
steps: Cumulative: last year's unpaid ₹80,000 is carried forward.
Total due = ₹1,60,000 before any equity dividend.

learn.reallife: Many Indian banks raise funds through preference shares, while retail investors on NSE mostly buy equity shares for voting rights and growth.

quiz.explain: Cumulative: both years' dividend (₹80,000 each) must be paid.

quiz.q: Shares that receive a share in surplus profits in addition to their fixed dividend are:
quiz.explain: Participating shares take part in surplus profits after equity dividend.

quiz.q: Under the Companies Act, 2013, which preference shares CANNOT be issued?
quiz.explain: Section 55 bars a company from issuing irredeemable preference shares.

quiz.explain: A share is movable property, transferable in the manner the articles provide.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a share with a debenture (loan)

quiz.explain: Non-cumulative shares lose the dividend for a year in which none is declared.

quiz.explain: Bearing the residual risk and controlling by vote makes them the real owners.
quiz.mistake: Thinks preference holders are the real owners

teach.praise: Spot on! Preference = fixed dividend and capital priority; equity = residual rights and voting power.

learn.hook: A company may be allowed ₹5 lakh of capital, offer ₹4 lakh, get applications for ₹3.6 lakh and collect even less. Each layer has its own name.
points: Authorised (registered or nominal) capital: the maximum capital a company is allowed to raise, stated in its Memorandum.
Issued capital: the part of authorised capital offered for subscription (including shares issued to vendors). Unissued capital: the rest.
Subscribed capital: the part of issued capital actually taken up. It may be 'subscribed and fully paid up' or 'subscribed but not fully paid up'.
Called-up capital: the amount on subscribed shares that the company has asked shareholders to pay; uncalled capital is the rest. Paid-up capital = called-up capital − calls in arrears.
Reserve capital: a portion of uncalled capital that the company, by special resolution, decides to call only on winding up.

example.q: Authorised: 50,000 shares of ₹10. Issued: 40,000. Subscribed: 36,000. ₹8 per share called; holders of 1,000 shares have not paid the last ₹2 call. Find each category.

learn.reallife: When an Indian company comes out with an IPO, it usually issues only part of its authorised capital; the prospectus spells out these layers.

topics.title: Share capital in the balance sheet and notes

learn.hook: Open any listed company's annual report: 'Share capital – Note 2'. Behind that one line sits a whole table. Let's read it like a pro.
points: Balance sheet (Schedule III): Equity and Liabilities → Shareholders' Funds → Share Capital, with details in Notes to Accounts.
Note on Share Capital shows: Authorised capital; Issued capital; Subscribed capital – (a) Subscribed and fully paid up, (b) Subscribed but not fully paid up (called-up less calls in arrears).
Amount in the balance sheet = subscribed and fully paid up + (subscribed but not fully paid up − calls in arrears) + share forfeiture account balance.
Calls in advance are not part of share capital; they are shown under Other Current Liabilities.
Securities premium is shown under Reserves and Surplus, not under Share Capital.

example.q: A company issued 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, fully called. All were subscribed. Calls in arrears are ₹5,000. Show share capital.

learn.reallife: The Companies Act, 2013 requires every Indian company to present its balance sheet in the Schedule III format, so investors everywhere see the same layout.

quiz.explain: They are owed back to shareholders until the call is made.

quiz.explain: Premium is a capital profit, kept in Reserves and Surplus.

quiz.q: In which part of the annual report are the details of authorised, issued and subscribed capital given?
quiz.explain: The balance sheet shows one line; the Note gives the breakdown.

teach.praise: Perfect! Share capital under Shareholders' Funds, with details in notes and calls in arrears deducted.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: where do calls in advance go – share capital or liabilities?

topics.title: Issue of shares at par: process and entries

learn.hook: An IPO opens: you apply with some money, get an allotment message, then pay calls. Each step is a journal entry in the company's books.
points: Process: issue of prospectus → receipt of applications → allotment → calls. The company must receive minimum subscription of 90% of the issue before allotting shares.
Shares may be issued for cash in a lump sum or in instalments (application, allotment, first call, final call). Issue at par means at face value.

Entries: Bank Dr / Share Application Cr; Share Application Dr / Share Capital Cr; Share Allotment Dr / Share Capital Cr; Bank Dr / Share Allotment Cr; Share First Call Dr / Share Capital Cr; Bank Dr / Share First Call Cr.
Without separate call accounts, money received on allotment and calls can be credited directly to Share Capital (Bank Dr / Share Capital Cr).

example.q: Mehta Ltd issues 10,000 equity shares of ₹10 at par: ₹3 on application, ₹4 on allotment, ₹3 on first and final call. All money is received. Find amounts at each stage.
steps: Application: 10,000 × 3 = ₹30,000 (Bank Dr / Share Application Cr; then transferred to Share Capital).
Allotment: 10,000 × 4 = ₹40,000 (Share Allotment Dr / Share Capital Cr; Bank Dr / Share Allotment Cr).

learn.reallife: During a popular IPO on NSE, ASBA blocks your application money in your own bank account until allotment – the company records it only when shares are allotted.

topics.title: Issue of shares at a premium; discount rule

learn.hook: Investors happily pay ₹12 for a ₹10 share of a strong company. That extra ₹2 can't be spent on anything you like – the law tells you where it may go.
points: Issue at premium: issue price above face value. The premium is credited to Securities Premium Account (Reserves and Surplus), usually collected with allotment.
Allotment with premium: Share Allotment A/c Dr (total) / Share Capital A/c Cr (capital part), Securities Premium A/c Cr (premium part).

Section 52 uses of securities premium: issuing fully paid bonus shares; writing off preliminary expenses; writing off expenses of, or commission paid or discount allowed on, any issue of shares or debentures; providing premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures; buy-back of own shares (Section 68).
Securities premium cannot be used to pay dividend.
Section 53: a company cannot issue shares at a discount; such issue is void. Exception: sweat equity shares (Section 54).

example.q: 10,000 shares of ₹10 issued at ₹12: ₹3 on application, ₹5 on allotment (including premium), ₹4 on first and final call. Show the allotment entry.
steps: Share Allotment Dr 50,000 / Share Capital Cr 30,000, Securities Premium Cr 20,000.
example.answer: Dr Share Allotment ₹50,000 / Cr Share Capital ₹30,000, Cr Securities Premium ₹20,000

learn.reallife: Hot IPOs on Dalal Street are priced well above the ₹10 or ₹1 face value; the difference sits in securities premium in the company's books.

quiz.explain: Any issue at discount is void except sweat equity under Section 54.

quiz.q: Securities premium is shown in the balance sheet under:
quiz.explain: It is a reserve of capital nature.

topics.title: Calls in arrears and calls in advance

learn.hook: Some shareholders pay late; a few eager ones pay early. The company tracks both in separate accounts.
points: Calls in arrears: amount called but not paid by some shareholders. Entry when receiving a call: Bank A/c Dr (amount received), Calls in Arrears A/c Dr (unpaid) / Share Call A/c Cr.
Calls in arrears are deducted from called-up capital in the Share Capital note.
Calls in advance: money received before a call is made. Entry: Bank A/c Dr / Calls in Advance A/c Cr.
When the call is later made: Calls in Advance A/c Dr / Share Call A/c Cr.
Calls in advance appear under Other Current Liabilities until adjusted. (Interest on these is outside this course.)

example.q: First call of ₹3 on 10,000 shares is made. Holders of 1,000 shares fail to pay. Record the receipt.
steps: Bank Dr 27,000; Calls in Arrears Dr 3,000 / Share First Call Cr 30,000.
example.answer: Bank ₹27,000 and Calls in Arrears ₹3,000 debited; Share First Call ₹30,000 credited.

learn.reallife: Just as some flat-buyers in a Noida housing project pay instalments late and some prepay, shareholders can fall into arrears or pay in advance.

items.text: Unpaid call money is debited to the Calls in ___ Account.
Money received before the call is made is credited to Calls in ___ Account.
Calls in advance are shown under Other ___ Liabilities.
Calls in arrears are ___ from called-up capital.

games.title: Arrears vs advance
items: Calls in arrears are part of the company's liabilities.
They are amounts receivable, deducted from called-up capital.
Calls in advance are a liability of the company.
The company owes them until adjusted against calls.
When a call is made, calls in advance are adjusted by debiting Calls in Advance A/c.
And crediting the Share Call A/c.
Calls in advance are added to share capital.
They are shown under Other Current Liabilities.

quiz.q: First call of ₹3 on 10,000 shares; holders of 1,000 shares fail to pay. Amount debited to Calls in Arrears:
quiz.explain: 1,000 × 3 = ₹3,000 remains unpaid.
quiz.mistake: Uses the number of shares as rupees

quiz.q: In the same case, cash received on the first call:
quiz.mistake: Assumes all call money was received

quiz.q: Entry when a shareholder pays the final call along with allotment (before the call is made):
options: Bank A/c Dr / Share Capital A/c Cr
Calls in Advance A/c Dr / Bank A/c Cr
Bank A/c Dr / Share Allotment A/c Cr, Calls in Advance A/c Cr
Bank A/c Dr / Share Final Call A/c Cr
quiz.explain: The extra amount is held in Calls in Advance until the call is made.
quiz.mistake: Credits the call account before it is due

quiz.q: When the final call is made later, the calls in advance are adjusted by:
options: Share Final Call A/c Dr / Calls in Advance A/c Cr
Calls in Advance A/c Dr / Bank A/c Cr
Share Capital A/c Dr / Calls in Advance A/c Cr
Calls in Advance A/c Dr / Share Final Call A/c Cr
quiz.explain: The advance is applied against the call money due.

quiz.q: Calls in advance appear in the balance sheet under:
quiz.explain: They are owed to shareholders until set off.

quiz.q: Called-up capital ₹5,00,000; calls in arrears ₹8,000; calls in advance ₹4,000. Paid-up capital shown in the share capital note:
quiz.explain: Paid-up = 5,00,000 − 8,000. Calls in advance are not part of share capital.
quiz.mistake: Adds calls in advance to capital

quiz.q: A shareholder holding 200 shares pays the final call of ₹2 per share along with allotment. Calls in advance:
quiz.mistake: Uses the number of shares as rupees

quiz.q: Calls in arrears are shown in the share capital note as:
quiz.explain: Paid-up capital = called-up capital − calls in arrears.

teach.ask: Gappu doesn't get calls in arrears and calls in advance. Explain both.
teach.praise: Neat! Arrears = called but unpaid (deducted); advance = paid early (a current liability).
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: where are calls in advance shown in the balance sheet?

learn.hook: A hot IPO is subscribed 30 times; a dull one limps to 92%. Each needs different handling of application money.
points: Under-subscription: applications are fewer than shares offered. If at least the minimum subscription (90%) is received, shares are allotted to all applicants.
Over-subscription: applications exceed shares offered. The company may (a) reject some applications and refund money, (b) allot pro-rata, or (c) combine both.

Pro-rata allotment: shares allotted in proportion to shares applied. Excess application money of pro-rata applicants is adjusted towards allotment (and calls, if the articles allow); any balance is refunded.
Entries: Share Application Dr / Share Capital Cr (allotted), Share Allotment Cr (excess adjusted), Bank Cr (refund).

example.q: A company offers 10,000 shares of ₹10: ₹3 on application, ₹4 on allotment, ₹3 on call. It receives applications for 15,000 shares and allots pro-rata. Find cash due on allotment.

learn.reallife: Big IPOs on NSE often see institutional, HNI and retail portions oversubscribed many times, leading to lottery or pro-rata allotment.

items.text: Refund to rejected applicants: Dr Share Application A/c, Cr ___ A/c.
Excess money of pro-rata applicants is first adjusted towards ___.
Application money on shares allotted is credited to ___ A/c.
Shares are allotted only if at least ___ of the issue is subscribed.

items.q: Applied 600, allotted 400: shares applied per share allotted

quiz.q: A company offers 10,000 shares and receives applications for 9,500. Minimum subscription is 90%. The company:
quiz.explain: 9,500 is 95% of the issue, above the 90% minimum, so all applicants get shares.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the whole issue must be subscribed

quiz.q: 10,000 shares offered (₹3 application, ₹4 allotment); applications for 15,000; pro-rata allotment. Cash due on allotment:
quiz.explain: Excess application money ₹15,000 is adjusted against allotment due ₹40,000.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to adjust the excess application money

quiz.q: Applications for 18,000 shares are received for 10,000 offered (₹3 application). Applications for 3,000 shares are rejected; the rest get pro-rata allotment. Refund:
quiz.explain: Only rejected applicants get a refund: 3,000 × 3.

quiz.q: In the same case, excess application money adjusted towards allotment:
quiz.explain: Pro-rata applicants applied for 15,000 shares and got 10,000; excess 5,000 × 3.

quiz.q: Applications for 25,000 shares for 10,000 offered, all allotted pro-rata (₹3 application, ₹4 allotment). The articles do not allow adjustment against calls. Amount refunded:
quiz.explain: Excess = 15,000 × 3 = 45,000; ₹40,000 adjusted against allotment; ₹5,000 refunded.

quiz.q: Pro-rata allotment means:
options: allotting full shares to the first applicants only
allotting shares in proportion to the shares applied for
allotting by lottery to a few
quiz.explain: Each pro-rata applicant gets a fixed fraction of what he applied for.

quiz.q: The entry for transferring excess application money to allotment is:
options: Share Allotment A/c Dr / Share Application A/c Cr
Bank A/c Dr / Share Allotment A/c Cr
Share Application A/c Dr / Share Allotment A/c Cr
Share Application A/c Dr / Bank A/c Cr
quiz.explain: Excess application money is moved from application to allotment.

quiz.q: X applied for 600 shares and was allotted 400 (₹3 application, ₹4 allotment). Amount X must pay on allotment:
quiz.explain: Excess on application = 200 × 3 = ₹600; allotment due 400 × 4 = ₹1,600; payable ₹1,000.

teach.ask: Gappu's IPO was oversubscribed. Explain how the company deals with extra applications.
teach.praise: Fantastic! Reject and refund some, allot pro-rata to others, and adjust their excess against allotment.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: what happens to extra application money of pro-rata applicants?

topics.title: Shares issued for consideration other than cash

learn.hook: A company buys a factory but pays in shares instead of cash. How many shares does the seller get?
points: A company may issue shares to vendors for assets or a business purchased. Entry 1: Assets A/c Dr / Vendor A/c Cr (purchase consideration).
Entry 2: Vendor A/c Dr / Share Capital A/c Cr (and Securities Premium A/c Cr if issued at a premium).
Number of shares = Purchase consideration ÷ Issue price per share.
When a business is bought: Assets Dr, Goodwill Dr (if consideration exceeds net assets) / Liabilities Cr, Vendor Cr, Capital Reserve Cr (if consideration is less than net assets).
Shares may also be issued to promoters for their services in forming the company; Share Capital is credited and the cost of their services is treated as part of formation (incorporation) costs.

example.q: A company buys machinery for ₹4,40,000 and pays by issuing equity shares of ₹10 at a premium of 10%. Find the number of shares and the entry.
steps: Vendor Dr 4,40,000 / Share Capital Cr 4,00,000, Securities Premium Cr 40,000.

learn.reallife: Indian tech companies acquiring smaller start-ups often pay part of the price in their own shares – a share-swap that is issue for consideration other than cash.

games.title: Non-cash issue
items: Number of shares to vendor = purchase consideration ÷ face value, even when issued at a premium.
Divide by the issue price, which includes the premium.
If purchase consideration exceeds net assets, the difference is goodwill.
The company pays extra for the business's reputation.
If purchase consideration is less than net assets, the difference is credited to capital reserve.
It is a capital profit.
Shares issued to vendors are not part of issued capital.
They are part of issued and subscribed capital.

quiz.q: Machinery of ₹4,40,000 is bought; shares of ₹10 are issued at 10% premium. Number of shares issued:
quiz.mistake: Divides by face value instead of issue price

quiz.q: In the same case, securities premium credited:
quiz.explain: 40,000 shares × ₹1 premium.

quiz.q: First entry on purchasing assets from a vendor (before issuing shares):
options: Vendor A/c Dr / Share Capital A/c Cr
Share Capital A/c Dr / Assets A/c Cr
Assets A/c Dr / Vendor A/c Cr
Assets A/c Dr / Share Capital A/c Cr
quiz.explain: First the liability to the vendor is recorded; then shares discharge it.
quiz.mistake: Credits share capital directly at purchase

quiz.q: Assets ₹6,00,000 and liabilities ₹1,00,000 of a business are taken over for a purchase consideration of ₹5,50,000. Goodwill:
quiz.explain: Net assets = ₹5,00,000; consideration exceeds it by ₹50,000.

quiz.q: Net assets of ₹5,00,000 are taken over for ₹4,80,000. The difference is credited to:
quiz.explain: Paying less than net assets gives a capital profit, credited to capital reserve.

quiz.q: A business is bought for ₹6,00,000, paid by issuing ₹100 shares at a 20% premium. Number of shares:
quiz.mistake: Divides by the face value of ₹100

quiz.q: Shares issued to promoters for their services in forming the company are credited to:
quiz.explain: Promoters receive shares, so Share Capital is credited; the services are treated as a formation cost.
quiz.mistake: Thinks shares to promoters are recorded as premium

quiz.q: Entry for issuing shares at par to a vendor for ₹3,00,000:
options: Share Capital A/c Dr / Vendor A/c Cr ₹3,00,000
Bank A/c Dr / Share Capital A/c Cr ₹3,00,000
Vendor A/c Dr / Bank A/c Cr ₹3,00,000
Vendor A/c Dr / Share Capital A/c Cr ₹3,00,000
quiz.explain: The vendor's claim is discharged by allotting shares.
quiz.mistake: Records a cash receipt that never happened

teach.ask: Gappu's company paid for a factory with shares. Explain the entries and how many shares are issued.
teach.praise: Great! Assets Dr / Vendor Cr, then Vendor Dr / Share Capital Cr, and shares = consideration ÷ issue price.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: should he divide by the face value or by the issue price?

topics.title: Private placement, ESOP and sweat equity

learn.hook: Not every share issue is a public IPO. Some go to a chosen few investors, some reward employees, and some pay for brains instead of cash.
points: Private placement (Section 42): offer of securities to a select group of persons (not the public) through a private placement offer letter. Under the rules, an offer may be made to at most 200 persons in a financial year, excluding qualified institutional buyers and employees under ESOP.

Employee Stock Option Plan, ESOP (Section 2(37)): an option given to directors, officers or employees of the company (or its holding/subsidiary) to buy or subscribe for shares at a future date at a predetermined price.
An option is a right, not an obligation; the employee decides whether to exercise it.

Sweat equity shares (Section 2(88)): shares issued by a company to its directors or employees at a discount or for consideration other than cash, for providing know-how, intellectual property rights or value additions. This is the only case where shares may be issued at a discount (Sections 53 and 54).

example.q: An employee holds ESOP options for 1,000 shares at an exercise price of ₹50 each. He exercises all of them. How much does the company receive?
steps: He pays the predetermined price for each share.

learn.reallife: Indian start-ups widely use ESOPs to attract talent – employees join on lower salaries hoping their options will be valuable after a funding round or IPO.

games.title: Term ↔ meaning
pairs: Offer to a select group of persons
Option to employees to buy shares at a predetermined price
Shares for know-how or value addition, at discount or non-cash
Offer to the general public through a prospectus

games.title: Special issues
items: Sweat equity shares may be issued at a discount.
They are the exception to the bar on discount issues.
An ESOP obliges the employee to buy the shares.
It is an option – a right, not an obligation.
Private placement is an offer to the general public.
It is an offer to a select group.
ESOPs can be offered to employees of a subsidiary company.
Directors, officers or employees of the company, its holding or subsidiary are covered.
Sweat equity rewards know-how or intellectual property provided to the company.
That is its purpose.

quiz.q: Issue of shares to a select group of persons, not to the public, is called:
quiz.explain: Section 42 governs offers to a selected group through a private placement offer letter.
quiz.mistake: Confuses private placement with a public issue

quiz.q: Under the private placement rules, an offer in a financial year can be made to at most how many persons (excluding QIBs and ESOP employees)?
quiz.explain: The limit is 200 persons in a financial year.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up with partnership or other limits

quiz.q: ESOP stands for:
quiz.explain: It gives employees an option to buy shares at a fixed future price.

quiz.q: An ESOP gives an employee:
options: an obligation to buy shares at market price
the right, but not the obligation, to buy shares at a predetermined price in future
quiz.explain: It is an option the employee may or may not exercise.

quiz.q: Sweat equity shares are issued:
options: to directors or employees at a discount or for non-cash consideration for know-how or value additions
to the public at a premium
quiz.explain: They reward intellectual contribution, not cash.
quiz.mistake: Confuses sweat equity with vendor shares

quiz.q: The only case in which a company may issue shares at a discount under the Companies Act, 2013 is:
quiz.explain: Section 53 bars discount issues except sweat equity under Section 54.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ESOP pricing is a discount issue

quiz.q: An employee exercises options for 1,000 shares at ₹50 each. Cash received by the company:
quiz.mistake: Uses face value instead of exercise price

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Shares issued under private placement are not offered to the general public.
Reason (R): Private placement is made through a private placement offer letter to identified persons.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: The offer letter goes only to identified persons, which is why the public is not invited.
quiz.mistake: Fails to connect the method with the restriction

teach.ask: Gappu's start-up wants to reward employees and a tech expert with shares. Explain ESOP, sweat equity and private placement.
teach.praise: Brilliant! ESOP for employees' options, sweat equity for know-how, and private placement for a select group.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: which of these can be issued at a discount?

learn.hook: Miss your calls repeatedly and the company can take your shares away – keeping what you already paid. That's forfeiture.
points: Forfeiture: cancellation of shares for non-payment of allotment or calls, after due notice, as per the articles. Money already received is not refunded.
Shares at par: Share Capital Dr (called-up amount) / Unpaid Allotment or Calls Cr / Share Forfeiture Cr (amount received).
Shares at premium, premium RECEIVED: Securities Premium is not touched; debit Share Capital with called-up amount.
Shares at premium, premium NOT received: also debit Securities Premium with the unpaid premium.
Pro-rata cases: excess application money already adjusted counts as received; find unpaid amounts carefully. Share Forfeiture balance is added to paid-up capital in the Share Capital note.

example.q: Raj holds 100 shares of ₹10 issued at par. He paid ₹3 on application and ₹4 on allotment but not the ₹3 final call. The shares are forfeited. Pass the entry.
steps: Unpaid call: 100 × 3 = ₹300 → credit Share Final Call.
example.answer: Share Capital Dr ₹1,000 / Share Final Call Cr ₹300, Share Forfeiture Cr ₹700

learn.reallife: Several listed Indian companies have forfeited partly-paid shares when holders ignored call notices after a rights issue.

items.text: On forfeiture, Share Capital is debited with the ___ amount.
Share Forfeiture is credited with the amount ___.
If premium was not received, ___ Premium is also debited.
Share Forfeiture balance is ___ to paid-up capital in the notes.

items.q: Applied 600, allotted 400 at ₹3 application: money received on application

quiz.q: 100 shares of ₹10 at par; ₹7 received; ₹3 final call unpaid; shares forfeited. Amount credited to Share Forfeiture:
quiz.explain: Forfeiture is credited with the money actually received: 100 × 7.

quiz.q: In the same case, Share Capital is debited with:
quiz.explain: Share Capital is debited with the called-up amount: 100 × 10.

quiz.q: 200 shares of ₹10 issued at ₹12 (₹2 premium in allotment). The holder paid application ₹3 and allotment ₹5 but not the final call ₹4. Forfeiture credit:
quiz.explain: Received towards capital = 3 + (5 − 2) = ₹6 per share; premium was received and stays.
quiz.mistake: Includes the premium received in forfeiture

quiz.q: 100 shares of ₹10 at ₹12 (premium ₹2 in allotment). Holder paid only application ₹3; failed allotment ₹5 and call ₹4. On forfeiture, Securities Premium is:
quiz.explain: Premium was credited on allotment but never received, so it is reversed: 100 × 2.
quiz.mistake: Leaves the unpaid premium in the books

quiz.q: In the same case, amount credited to Share Forfeiture:
quiz.explain: Only the application money of ₹3 per share was received.

quiz.q: X applied for 600 shares and was allotted 400 (₹10 shares: ₹3 application, ₹4 allotment, ₹3 call). Excess application money was adjusted against allotment. X paid nothing more, and his shares were forfeited after the call. Amount credited to Share Forfeiture:
quiz.explain: All money X paid (600 × 3 = ₹1,800) is forfeited, including the excess already adjusted.
quiz.mistake: Counts only application money on allotted shares

quiz.q: In the same case, unpaid allotment money credited to Share Allotment A/c on forfeiture:
quiz.explain: Allotment due 400 × 4 = 1,600 less excess 200 × 3 = 600.

quiz.q: Balance of Share Forfeiture Account (not yet reissued) is shown in the balance sheet:
options: added to paid-up capital in the Share Capital note
quiz.explain: It represents money received on capital, so it is added.
quiz.mistake: Treats it as a reserve or liability

teach.ask: Gappu's shareholder didn't pay the call and the shares were forfeited. Explain the entry.
teach.praise: Spot on! Debit capital with called-up, credit unpaid calls, and credit forfeiture with money received.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: when must Securities Premium be debited on forfeiture?

learn.hook: Forfeited shares are back with the company. It can sell them again – even cheaply – but only so cheaply.
points: Forfeited shares may be re-issued at par, at a premium or at a discount. The discount on re-issue cannot exceed the amount forfeited on those shares.
Entry: Bank Dr (amount received), Share Forfeiture Dr (discount allowed) / Share Capital Cr (paid-up value credited); premium, if any, to Securities Premium Cr.
After re-issue, the remaining forfeited amount on re-issued shares is a capital profit: Share Forfeiture Dr / Capital Reserve Cr.
If only some forfeited shares are re-issued, transfer to capital reserve only the gain on those shares: (forfeited amount per share × shares re-issued) − discount allowed.
Balance sheet: capital reserve goes to Reserves and Surplus; any forfeiture balance on shares not re-issued stays in the Share Capital note.

example.q: 100 forfeited shares (₹10 each; ₹700 forfeited) are re-issued at ₹8 per share fully paid. Pass entries.
steps: Bank Dr 800; Share Forfeiture Dr 200 / Share Capital Cr 1,000.
Share Forfeiture Dr 500 / Capital Reserve Cr 500.

learn.reallife: When a company re-issues forfeited shares cheaply, it is a bit like an airline reselling a cancelled seat – it already kept part of the first passenger's money.

games.title: Re-issue: steps
items: Forfeit the shares and credit Share Forfeiture
Re-issue shares and debit any discount to Share Forfeiture
Find the balance of forfeiture on re-issued shares
Transfer that balance to Capital Reserve

items.q: Forfeited ₹700 on 100 shares; max discount per share
Forfeited ₹6 each; 150 re-issued with ₹1 discount each: capital reserve

quiz.q: 100 shares (₹10) forfeited after ₹7 was received are re-issued at ₹8 fully paid. Amount debited to Share Forfeiture for discount:
quiz.explain: Discount ₹2 per share × 100.

quiz.q: In the same case, amount transferred to Capital Reserve:
quiz.explain: Forfeited ₹700 less discount ₹200.

quiz.q: Shares of ₹10 were forfeited after ₹7 per share was received. The maximum discount per share allowed on their re-issue is:
quiz.explain: Discount on re-issue cannot exceed the amount forfeited on each share.
quiz.mistake: Uses the unpaid amount (₹3) or thinks no discount is allowed

quiz.q: Forfeited shares (₹10 each) are re-issued at ₹11 fully paid. The extra ₹1 per share is credited to:
quiz.explain: Any amount above face value on re-issue is premium.

quiz.q: 200 shares (₹6 per share forfeited, total ₹1,200) were forfeited. 150 are re-issued at ₹9 fully paid. Capital reserve:
quiz.explain: Forfeiture on 150 shares = 900; discount 150; capital reserve = 750. The ₹300 on 50 unissued shares stays.

quiz.q: In the same case, the balance left in Share Forfeiture after transfer:
quiz.explain: Relates to the 50 shares not yet re-issued: 50 × 6.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the account is fully closed

quiz.q: Capital reserve arising on re-issue of forfeited shares is shown under:
quiz.explain: It is a capital profit and part of reserves.

quiz.q: Entry to transfer the gain on re-issued forfeited shares:
options: Capital Reserve A/c Dr / Share Forfeiture A/c Cr
Share Forfeiture A/c Dr / General Reserve A/c Cr
Share Forfeiture A/c Dr / Securities Premium A/c Cr
Share Forfeiture A/c Dr / Capital Reserve A/c Cr
quiz.explain: The surplus is a capital profit, so it goes to Capital Reserve.

teach.ask: Gappu re-issued forfeited shares at a discount. Explain the limit and where the balance goes.
teach.praise: Excellent! Discount up to the forfeited amount, and the balance on re-issued shares to capital reserve.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: what is the most discount he can allow on re-issue?
